newsitem.title: UK: Globe Theatre offers taste of Shakespeare's London.
newsitem.headline: Globe Theatre offers taste of Shakespeare's London.

text.p: Britain's Globe Theatre officially opened on Thursday in an exquisite reconstruction of the simple wooden playhouse that first rang with Shakespeare's plays 400 years ago.

Under blustery skies and all but drowned out by drilling workmen, artistic director Mark Rylance said the open-topped Globe was the closest possible thing to the Elizabethan playhouse that Shakespeare had called home.

"This here is the official opening of the Globe Theatre," Rylance told reporters as workers scurried to finish the job. "This is our best guess about what Shakespeare's Globe was like. It has been built in the same manner and form."
Henry V will be staged next Tuesday.
Standing room costs a penny, in a nod to Elizabethan days but will cost five pounds ($8) when the theatre is up and running.

"This is exhilarating theatre. You can wander around, eat or lean on the stage so Shakespeare becomes far less elevated and more like the passionate entertainment it once was," said spokeswoman Lucy Beevor.

The Globe sits on the south bank of the Thames opposite St Paul's Cathedral. A wooden round, the central playhouse is open to the elements and the audience must either stand, meander or sit on hard wooden benches.
Seven artists built the stage over three weeks, using gold leaf and 16th-century pigments to create an ornate, pillared platform for the British and U.S. actors.

"Performing here feels like being a pip inside an orange. You have faces at your ankles, people packed in the galleries and the eyes are all so close you are entirely enclosed," said actor Patrick Godfrey.
The Globe was the brainchild of the late U.S. actor-director Sam Wanamaker, who devoted a quarter of a century to bring Shakespeare back to his London site.
Foundations were laid in 1987 and the 30-million pound ($49 million) project is expected to be complete by September 1999, the 400th anniversary of the first recorded performance at the Globe.
The cast says the Globe will be far more than a candy-floss reincarnation of bygone times.

"In my indulgent romantic moments, in my hand-stitched costumes, I do feel the shadows of the past but this is no theme park or museum theatre," said David Fielder, who plays the Welsh captain Fluellen next week.
"This is not an attempt to rediscover a lost time but to use the same vessel and re-mint it for now."
The first feet to tread the stage on Tuesday will be those of Vincent Brimble, who will appear as the comic Mistress Quickly and quickly kiss a fellow actor in the all-male performance of Henry V.

"It may take some time for the audience to settle down from the kiss but my daughter is already mortified at the very thought of it," said Brimble. "I have been in the business a long time but it is still a thrill to be the first person in a performance that is a real first."
